'''''Philadelphus coronarius''''' ('''sweet mock orange''',<ref name="mohlenbrock 2013"/> '''English dogwood'''<ref name="welch&grant2011"/>) is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Hydrangeaceae, [[native plant|native]] to the [[Caucasus]] and northeastern Turkey.<ref>{{cite web |title=Philadelphus coronarius L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:792194-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=18 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

==Description==
It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|3|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|2.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} wide, with toothed leaves and bowl-shaped white flowers with prominent stamens. In the species the blooms are abundant and very fragrant, but less so in the cultivars.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=Royal Horticultural Society A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants |location=London |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |year=2008 |pages=1136 |isbn=978-1405332965}}</ref> It may resemble, but is not closely related to, varieties of the similarly named [[dogwood]], which is the common name for ''[[Cornus]]'' in the family [[Cornaceae]].

It can be distinguished from other species of the genera by noting its high fragrance, [[Glabrous leaves|glabrous]] [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]], and lower surface of its leaves being only partially pubescent at the nerves (and not throughout).<ref name="mohlenbrock 2013"/>

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''coronarius'' means "used for garlands".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref>

==Distribution==
The plant is determined to be native to the areas of [[Turkey]], [[Transcaucasus]], and [[North Caucasus]].<ref name="powo"/>{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The idea of southern European origin had been floated by botanists in the past, and persist in some current literature by non-botanists.<ref name="PerfumeHB1997"/> Linnaeus who suggested Verona, Italy,{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=100}} however, Hu (1954) already saw no evidence of the plant spontaneously occurring in Spain, Italy, etc., even though British predecessors [[W. J. Bean]] (d. 1947) nd [[Alfred Rehder]] (d. 1949) had been supportive of the hypothesis.{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=100}} The Kew Garden's current POWO database excludes Europe from place of origin.<ref name="powo"/>}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Another (outdated) idea is that the Japanese species [[Philadelphus satsumi|P. satsumi]] was a subspecies of ''P. corronarius'', and this was the first to be introduced into Europe, suggested by [[Heinrich Schrader (botanist)|Schrader]] (1838)<ref>Schrader (1838) Linnea '''12''' (40) apud Hu (bibliog.)</ref>{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=100}} The Japanese (native, endemic) taxon is currently accepted as species in its own right.<ref name="powo-P.satsumi"/>}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Likewise, it is a now rejected taxonomy that was suggested by [[Karl Maximovich|Maximowicz]] (1867) ''Revisio Hydrangearum Asiae Orientalis'', which treated all Japanese and continental Asian ''Philadelphus'' as [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] of ''P. coronarius''.{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=281}} Maximowicz (like Schrader) also advanced the Japanese origin to the plants found in Europe, according to {{illm|Shirō Kitamura|ja|北村四郎}} (1974), who in turn supported the idea, though the conventional wisdom at the time was that the species was of uncertain origin.<ref name="kitamura1974"/>}}  It has spreads to wide parts of Europe, also Eastern Canada (Quebec and half of Ontario) and U.S. (Atlantic Coast to Georgia, the South, Midwest)<!--see map--><ref name="powo"/>

In [[1562]] the plant was introduced from Turkey into Europe by [[Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq]] returning to [[Holy Roman Empire]] from his ambassadorship to the [[sultan]]<ref name="coats1965"/><ref name="welch&grant2011"/> Around the same period, the [[lilac]] was introduced from the same general area (Middle East), and confusingly both called ''syringa'' (literally pan pipe, or pipe),<ref name="coats1965"/><ref name="welch&grant2011"/> not because the flowers etc. were particularly similar but because they both had hollowed stems and were used for manufacturing pipes by the Turks.<ref name="welch&grant2011"/>

Thus pre-[[Linnaean taxonomy|Linnaean]] authors referred to ''Philadelphus spp.'' as ''Syrigna alba''.{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=313}} [[Carolus Clusius]] when he illustrated the plant in his ''Libri Picturati'' (1576) used the name ''Syrigna flore alba''<ref name="clusius2017"/> but he also developed the name  ''Frutex coronarius'' which only he used{{sfnp|Hu|1954|p=278}}{{sfnp|McKelvey|1928|p=514}} in ''Rariorum plantarum historia'' (1601).<ref name="curtis1797"/>

They were known to be grown in Austria and Hungary in the 16th century,{{Refn|clusius (1601?) apud {{harvp|Hu|1954|p=100}}.}} and Clusius found them in a Belgian garden, later introducing the plant to Spain.<ref name="clusius2017"/> In England, [[John Gerard]] professed to growing the characteristically fragranced plant in profusion in his ''Herball'' (1597),{{sfnp|Coats|1965|pp=334–335}} but he used the name ''Syrigna alba'', which confused some writers into thinking they were white-flowered lilacs, even though Gerard actually meant the mock oranges.<ref name="curtis1797"/><ref name="mcKelvey1928"/>

==Cultivation==
It is a sweetly scented white blossom suitable for temperate climate cultivation as [[ornamental plant]] for [[garden]]s.{{cn|date=July 2025}} It blooms in spring (April to May) in the American South,<ref name="welch&grant2011"/> perhaps later in the temperate Midwest (April to May).<ref name="mohlenbrock 2013"/> It tolerates cold as well as heat and drought.<ref name="mohlenbrock 2013"/> But [[Niels Ebbesen Hansen|Hansen]] considered it too winter-tender for [[South Dakota]] as the shrub died off to the ground during the cold.<ref name="hansen1901"/>

It is easily propagated by cuttings, by division, from self-sewn seedling, etc.<ref name="welch&grant2011"/>

There are a large number of named [[cultivar]]s.<ref name="welch&grant2011"/> It also interbreeds readily with other species. A number of  ''P. coronarius'' × ''[[Philadelphus microphyllus|P. microphyllus]]'' have been introduced by the Lemoine Nursery ([[Nice, France]]).<ref name="welch&grant2011"/>

The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:-
* ''P. coronarius'' 'Aureus'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Philadelphus coronarius'' 'Aureus'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/98429/philadelphus-coronarius-aureus/details|access-date=21 July 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130607110852/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=1422|archive-date=7 June 2013|url-status=live}}</ref>
*''P. coronarius'' 'Variegatus'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Philadelphus coronarius'' 'Variegatus'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/98429/philadelphus-coronarius-aureus/details|access-date=21 July 2024}}</ref>

The 16th century botanist Gerard considered the fragrance to be too intense and it disturbed his sleep.{{sfnp|Coats|1965|pp=334–335}}<ref name="curtis1797"/><ref name="mcKelvey1928"/> [[Edward Augustus Bowles|E. A. Bowles]] claimed it triggered [[allergic reaction]], with [[hay fever]]-like symptoms.<ref name="coats1965"/>

== Other uses ==
The mock orange blossom, said to resemble the smell of orange blossoms, has been used in modern [[Perfume|perfumery]], though the [[essential oil]] is nowadays usually synthesized.{{sfnp|Coats|1965|p=244}}<ref name="PerfumeHB1997"/> Once marketed as "oil of syringa" or "oil of false jasmine" (in Europe), it had been used in the manufacture of cheap [[pomade]] called "orange-blossom pomade" in the [[South of France]].<ref name="askinson1892"/> In the present-day, one suggested use is as [[potpourri]].<ref name="PerfumeHB1997"/>

The blossom tea can also be made, according to English botanical painter [[Alice Margaret Coats]].{{sfnp|Coats|1965|p=244}} Such use as tea occurs locally in the [[Baltic countries]] ([[Latvia]] and [[Estonia]]) according to current literature.{{Refn|Tiţă, I; Mogoşanu, G.D., Tiţă, M.G.(2009) ''Ethnomedicinal inventory of medicinal plants from the south-west of Romania'' and Prūse et al. (2021b)<ref name="pruse-etal2021b"/> ''apud'' Paniagua-Zambrana et al. (2025)<ref name="paniagua-zambrana-etal2025"/>}}

Coats also suggested that the leaves of the plant can add [[cucumber]]-like flavor to a beverage.{{sfnp|Coats|1965|p=244}}
